name: Bytecode and Platform Independence
overview: A .class file travels light. Follow one Java program across platforms, then use javap to see what javac packed.

sections.title: What javac produces
sections.content: The compiler stores JVM instructions and metadata in a .class file. Its 0xCAFEBABE header identifies the format. Other checks decide whether the file can actually run.

sections.title: Why one file can travel
sections.content: A compatible JVM on each operating system understands the same bytecode. Keep the target Java version in mind and check for dependencies on native libraries or OS-specific behavior.

images.alt: From Java source to machine code
images.caption: The compiler creates bytecode. A JVM on each target platform runs it.

sections.title: How the JVM runs it
sections.content: Verification checks bytecode constraints during linking. A JVM can interpret instructions and compile frequently executed code to machine code. Measure startup and steady-state performance separately.

codeExamples.title: Compiling and Viewing Bytecode
codeExamples.description: Commands to compile Java code to bytecode and inspect the generated bytecode instructions using javap.
codeExamples.code:
# Compile Java source to bytecode
javac HelloWorld.java

# View bytecode instructions
javap -c HelloWorld

# View detailed class information
javap -v HelloWorld

keyPoints: Run javap -c on a tiny class and point to where it loads a value, does work, and returns.

references.title: Javap - The Java Class File Disassembler

interviewQA.question: Does the CPU run Java bytecode directly?
interviewQA.answer: Normally the JVM interprets it or compiles it into machine code for that CPU.

interviewQA.question: How do you inspect bytecode?
interviewQA.answer: Run javap -c followed by the compiled class name.
